title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
Imagine someone hands you a coin and insists it is fair. You decide to flip it ten times and check whether either side appears suspiciously often. Nine flips come up heads. You would probably question the coin. But how much evidence do those nine heads provide?
A p-value helps answer that question by asking us to imagine a world where the coin really is fair. The difficulty is keeping that imagined world separate from what we want to know about the actual coin.

title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
Start by assuming fairness
Our starting claim, called the null hypothesis, is that each flip has a 50% chance of heads. We also assume the flips are independent: one result does not affect the next. We fix the number of flips at ten before starting.
Even a fair coin will not always produce five heads and five tails. Randomness creates uneven results. The useful question is how often it would produce an imbalance at least as large as the one we observed.
That is the idea behind a p-value: assuming the null hypothesis and the statistical model hold, calculate the probability of a test result at least as extreme as the observed one. NIST’s definition makes this conditional starting point explicit.

title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
Counting the surprising outcomes
Because we decided to check for bias toward either side, nine tails would be just as suspicious as nine heads. This is a two-sided test. Our measure of extremeness is the distance from five heads, so the outcomes we count are zero, one, nine, and ten heads.
Each flip has two possible outcomes, so ten independent fair flips have \(2^{10}=1,024\) equally likely sequences. The counted outcomes are:



Number of heads
Number of possible sequences




0
1


1
10


9
10


10
1


Total
22



There are ten sequences with nine heads because the single tail can appear in any of ten positions. The same reasoning gives ten sequences with one head. Therefore,
\[
p = \frac{1+10+10+1}{1024} = \frac{22}{1024} \approx 0.0215.
\]
In repeated sets of ten fair flips, about 2.15% would be at least this unbalanced. We include ten heads because it would be even more extreme than nine. Counting only the exact result would leave out outcomes that provide stronger evidence against fairness.
Source: exact calculation for this hypothetical example; no observed dataset is used.

title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
Why the interpretation feels backward
The tempting conclusion is: “There is only a 2.15% chance that the coin is fair.” But the calculation began by assuming fairness. It never assigned a probability to that assumption.
The distinction is between the probability of evidence given a claim and the probability of a claim given evidence. Knowing an animal is a dog makes it certain that it is a mammal. Knowing it is a mammal does not make it certain that it is a dog. Reversing the condition changes the question.
We naturally start with the evidence and ask what to believe. A p-value works in the other direction, starting with a proposed explanation and asking how unusual the evidence would be. The American Statistical Association’s statement specifically warns against interpreting it as the probability that a hypothesis is true.

title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
What should we conclude?
The nine heads give us a reason to question the fair-coin model. They do not prove the coin is biased: unusual outcomes sometimes happen under a correct model.
Researchers often compare p-values with 0.05, a conventional cutoff described in the NIST handbook. In otherwise comparable studies, results of 0.049 and 0.051 provide similar evidence despite falling on opposite sides of the cutoff. The ASA also cautions that a p-value does not measure an effect’s size or practical importance. For example, a hypothetical study might detect a tiny wage increase with a large sample; deciding whether that increase matters requires examining its size.

title: What does a p-value actually tell us?
text:
Reproduce the calculation
This Python code uses only the standard library. It counts all outcomes at least as far from five heads as the observed nine heads.
from math import comb

n = 10
observed_heads = 9
expected_heads = n / 2

extreme_counts = [
    k for k in range(n + 1)
    if abs(k - expected_heads) >= abs(observed_heads - expected_heads)
]
extreme_sequences = sum(comb(n, k) for k in extreme_counts)
p_value = extreme_sequences / (2 ** n)

print(extreme_counts)     # [0, 1, 9, 10]
print(extreme_sequences)  # 22
print(p_value)            # 0.021484375
For our coin, the takeaway is precise: if it were fair and the flips independent, results at least this unbalanced would occur about 2.15% of the time. That is useful evidence when judging fairness, while leaving uncertainty about the coin itself.

title: Which data skills should I learn first?
text:
Learning data analysis comes with a long shopping list: Excel, SQL, Python, R, and several dashboard tools. Trying to learn all of them at once is a good way to finish none of them. If I had a few weeks to prepare for an analyst role, which skill would I work on first?
To make that choice less arbitrary, I used R’s rvest package to collect 50 job postings from DataAnalyst.com. I looked for six familiar tools and counted how often employers mentioned each one.

title: Which data skills should I learn first?
text:
A small, focused sample
The collection took place on September 21, 2026, Pacific time. I used the first page of the site’s entry-level category, which labels roles as requiring zero to three years of experience. I kept active listings with “data analyst” in the title, excluded senior and leadership titles, removed duplicates, and took the first 50 qualifying listings in the displayed order. The board’s publication dates ran from May 14 to September 8, 2026.
For each job, rvest extracted the responsibilities and requirements. I left out company descriptions and related-job suggestions, since those could mention skills unrelated to the position. Each skill counted once per posting, even if it appeared several times. “PowerBI” and “Power BI” counted as the same tool. I also reviewed the matched text to check that words such as “Excel” referred to software.
The public pages needed no login, and the site’s robots.txt had no disallowed paths at collection. Requests were spaced at least three seconds apart, and the pages were saved locally so rerunning the analysis would not repeatedly contact the website.

title: Which data skills should I learn first?
text:
What showed up most often?



Skill mentions in the sampled postings. Each posting can mention multiple tools, so percentages do not sum to 100%. Source: DataAnalyst.com; collected September 21, 2026 (Pacific time).






Table 1: Mentions in responsibilities or requirements

SQL appeared in 38 of the 50 postings (76%). That makes it the clearest starting point among the six tools I checked. Excel appeared in 28 postings, while Python appeared in 22. The gap matters when study time is limited: I would want to be comfortable working with tables before adding another language to my list.
The tools also overlap. 20 postings mentioned both SQL and Python, and 23 mentioned at least one of Tableau or Power BI. These are useful combinations to practice, although a mention might describe a preferred skill or one of several acceptable tools. It does not always mean the employer requires it.

title: Which data skills should I learn first?
text:
How I would use this
I would start with a small SQL project: take a sales dataset, join the customer and order tables, and calculate monthly revenue. Then I would check the totals in Excel and write a short explanation of what changed. That gives me something concrete to discuss in an interview.
Once that feels manageable, I would choose the next tool from the jobs I actually want. For a role mentioning Python, I could automate the same cleaning steps. For a dashboard role, I could turn the results into a simple Tableau or Power BI report. There is little reason to learn both dashboard tools immediately just because they appear on a general skills list.
This sample has limits. It comes from one board, includes older listings, and contains 39 remote roles. Its entry-level label may also be imperfect. Keyword counts measure mentions, not proficiency or the effect of a skill on getting hired. A low count for R here does not make it unhelpful in research or economics.
For this sample, my first investment would be SQL, supported by Excel practice. After that, I would use a shortlist of actual target jobs to decide what to learn next.

title: Which data skills should I learn first?
text:
Data and code
The GitHub project folder contains the saved pages, cleaned data, results, and a README with replication instructions. Download the job data or skill counts. The code below uses rvest for extraction and base R for counting and plotting. See the rvest documentation for the scraping functions.






NoteR code: collect and clean the postings





# Run from blog/posts/post2: Rscript code/scrape.R
# Default: reuse saved HTML. --live downloads into a NEW dated snapshot folder.
library(rvest)
dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
live <- "--live" %in% commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
cache <- if (live) file.path("data", paste0("snapshot-", format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d-%H%M%S"))) else "data/raw"
dir.create(cache, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
base_url <- "https://www.dataanalyst.com"
listing_url <- paste0(base_url, "/job-experience/entry-level-data-analyst-jobs")

# Three seconds between requests; no retries or access restriction workarounds.
get_page <- function(url, name) {
  path <- file.path(cache, name)
  if (file.exists(path)) return(read_html(path))
  if (!live) stop("Saved HTML missing: restore data/raw or use --live after reviewing site rules.")
  Sys.sleep(3)
  message("Reading ", url)
  page <- read_html(url)
  xml2::write_html(page, path)
  page
}

# Check this small site's robots rules before any new collection.
if (live) {
  rules <- readLines(paste0(base_url, "/robots.txt"), warn = FALSE)
  writeLines(rules, file.path(cache, "robots.txt"))
  disallow <- grep("^Disallow:", rules, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
  if (any(nzchar(trimws(sub("^[^:]+:", "", disallow))))) {
    stop("Robots rules changed: review them before collecting any job pages.")
  }
  writeLines(format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE), file.path(cache, "collected_at.txt"))
}

page <- get_page(listing_url, "listing.html")
cards <- html_elements(page, "a.cms-jobs-counter")
field <- function(selector) html_text2(html_element(cards, selector))
jobs <- data.frame(
  title = trimws(field("h3")), company = trimws(field(".card-link-home")),
  location = field(".card-job-category-wrapper-location .card-job-category-text"),
  workplace = field(".card-job-category-wrapper-workplace .card-job-category-text"),
  experience = field(".card-job-category-wrapper-experience .card-job-category-text"),
  published = field(".card-job-category-wrapper-published .card-job-category-text"),
  status = field(".card-job-category-text-expired"),
  url = xml2::url_absolute(html_attr(cards, "href"), base_url)
)
stopifnot(nrow(jobs) > 0, !anyNA(jobs$title), !anyNA(jobs$url))
# Define the sample before reading skill frequencies: first 50 matching cards,
# in the site's displayed order, on this single listing page. No pagination.
jobs$eligible <- jobs$experience == "0 - 3 years" & jobs$status == "Active" &
  grepl("data analyst", jobs$title, ignore.case = TRUE) &
  !grepl("\\b(senior|sr|lead|principal|manager|director)\\b", jobs$title, ignore.case = TRUE)
jobs$eligible[is.na(jobs$eligible)] <- FALSE
write.csv(jobs, "data/listing_audit.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
jobs <- jobs[jobs$eligible & !duplicated(jobs$url) &
               !duplicated(paste(tolower(jobs$company), tolower(jobs$title), jobs$location)), ]
jobs <- head(jobs, 50)
jobs$eligible <- NULL
jobs$description <- jobs$requirements <- NA_character_
for (i in seq_len(nrow(jobs))) {
  slug <- sub(".*/", "", jobs$url[i])
  detail <- get_page(jobs$url[i], paste0(slug, ".html"))
  # Only responsibilities and requirements; exclude company bios and related jobs.
  jobs$description[i] <- html_text2(html_element(detail, ".rich-text-block-3"))
  jobs$requirements[i] <- html_text2(html_element(detail, ".rich-text-block-4"))
  if (is.na(jobs$description[i]) || is.na(jobs$requirements[i]) ||
      nchar(jobs$description[i]) + nchar(jobs$requirements[i]) < 100) {
    stop("Missing job text: inspect ", jobs$url[i])
  }
}
jobs$collected_at_utc <- readLines(file.path(cache, "collected_at.txt"), warn = FALSE)[1]
write.csv(jobs, "data/jobs.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
message("Saved ", nrow(jobs), " jobs; cache: ", cache)









NoteR code: count skills and create the chart





# Run from blog/posts/post2: Rscript code/analyze.R
# No website requests: all analysis uses the saved CSV.
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
jobs <- read.csv("data/jobs.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
stopifnot(nrow(jobs) > 0, !anyDuplicated(jobs$url),
          !anyNA(jobs$description), !anyNA(jobs$requirements))
text <- paste(jobs$description, jobs$requirements)
# Word boundaries avoid counting SQL inside NoSQL and R inside other words.
# Excel is case sensitive to avoid the ordinary verb "excel"; R is uppercase.
patterns <- c(SQL = "(?i)\\bSQL\\b", Excel = "\\bExcel\\b",
              Python = "(?i)\\bPython\\b", R = "\\bR\\b",
              Tableau = "(?i)\\bTableau\\b", `Power BI` = "(?i)\\bPower\\s*BI\\b")
flags <- sapply(patterns, function(p) grepl(p, text, perl = TRUE))
required_flags <- sapply(patterns, function(p) grepl(p, jobs$requirements, perl = TRUE))
counts <- data.frame(skill = names(patterns), jobs = colSums(flags),
                     percent = 100 * colMeans(flags),
                     requirements_section_jobs = colSums(required_flags), row.names = NULL)
counts <- counts[order(-counts$jobs, counts$skill), ]
write.csv(counts, "results/skill_counts.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(cbind(jobs[c("company", "title", "url")], flags),
          "results/job_skill_flags.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")

# Short contexts make it possible to review every keyword match.
audit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(patterns), function(skill) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(jobs)), function(i) {
    matches <- gregexpr(patterns[[skill]], text[i], perl = TRUE)[[1]]
    if (matches[1] < 0) return(NULL)
    data.frame(company = jobs$company[i], title = jobs$title[i], skill = skill,
               context = substring(text[i], pmax(1, matches - 70), matches + 100),
               url = jobs$url[i])
  }))
}))
write.csv(audit, "results/match_audit.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
metrics <- c(sample_size = nrow(jobs), companies = length(unique(jobs$company)),
             sql_and_python = sum(flags[, "SQL"] & flags[, "Python"]),
             either_visualization = sum(flags[, "Tableau"] | flags[, "Power BI"]),
             remote = sum(jobs$workplace == "Remote"))
write.csv(data.frame(metric = names(metrics), value = unname(metrics)),
          "results/metrics.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# One simple chart, with both percentages and job counts.
png("results/skills.png", width = 1600, height = 960, res = 180)
par(mar = c(5, 6, 5, 3), family = "sans", bg = "white", col.axis = "#344054")
plot_counts <- counts[nrow(counts):1, ]
y <- barplot(plot_counts$percent, horiz = TRUE, names.arg = plot_counts$skill,
             las = 1, xlim = c(0, 115), axes = FALSE, border = NA,
             col = ifelse(plot_counts$skill == counts$skill[1], "#216B6B", "#A6C5C5"),
             xlab = "Share of sampled job postings mentioning the skill (%)")
axis(1, at = seq(0, 100, 20))
text(plot_counts$percent + 2, y,
     labels = sprintf("%.0f%% (%d/%d)", plot_counts$percent, plot_counts$jobs, nrow(jobs)),
     adj = 0, cex = 0.9, col = "#243746")
title("Which skills show up most often?", adj = 0, col.main = "#243746")
collection_date <- format(as.POSIXct(jobs$collected_at_utc[1], tz = "UTC"),
                          tz = "America/Los_Angeles", format = "%Y-%m-%d")
mtext(sprintf("%d DataAnalyst.com postings | %s (Pacific time)",
              nrow(jobs), collection_date),
      side = 3, line = 1, adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = "#52616B")
dev.off()
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = "results/session-info.txt")
print(counts, row.names = FALSE)
print(metrics)

title: Home prices fell, but mortgage payments stayed high
text:
By the end of 2024, the median price of a new U.S. home was slightly lower than in early 2021 after accounting for inflation. Yet a buyer financing that home would face a monthly mortgage payment about 52% higher, also after inflation.
I asked whether falling new-home prices brought monthly mortgage payments back toward their early-2021 level. To answer that question, I compared sale prices, mortgage rates, and consumer prices from 2021 through 2024. Three charts show why the decline in sale prices brought only partial relief to someone taking out a new loan.

title: Home prices fell, but mortgage payments stayed high
section: Home prices gave back some of their gains
text:
Home prices gave back some of their gains



Figure 1. Nominal and CPI-adjusted median new-home sale prices. Both series are indexed to 100 in 2021 Q1. The vertical axis starts at 80 to show changes more clearly.


The median new-home sale price climbed from $355,000 in early 2021 to $442,600 in late 2022. It ended 2024 at $419,300, down 5.3% from that peak.
That still looks expensive compared with 2021. But dollars bought less by 2024. Adjusting for consumer-price inflation puts the final price at about $349,310 in early-2021 dollars—1.6% below its starting point. The inflation-adjusted decline from late 2022 was 10.7%.
For a buyer paying cash, that comparison is encouraging. A buyer borrowing most of the purchase price faces another number.

title: Home prices fell, but mortgage payments stayed high
section: A new mortgage cost much more
text:
A new mortgage cost much more



Figure 2. Quarterly average 30-year fixed mortgage rates. Weekly observations are assigned to the quarter of their publication date and averaged equally.


The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 2.88% in the first quarter of 2021. By the final quarter of 2024, it was 6.63%. Rates had eased from their late-2023 high, but borrowing was still considerably more expensive than at the start of the period.
A lower sale price reduces the loan balance. A higher rate raises the payment on every dollar borrowed. To see which change mattered more, I put them together.

title: Home prices fell, but mortgage payments stayed high
text:
The monthly bill stayed high



Figure 3. Illustrative monthly principal-and-interest payments, expressed in 2021 Q1 dollars. The dashed line holds the mortgage rate at its 2021 Q1 average while allowing prices and CPI to change. Both payment series use the same loan assumptions.


For each quarter, I calculated the payment on a median-priced new home with a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed mortgage at that quarter’s average rate. The chart shows principal and interest in early-2021 dollars.
The monthly payment rose from $1,178 in early 2021 to $2,011 in late 2022, then fell to $1,791 at the end of 2024. That was still about $612 more per month than at the start, in the same purchasing power. In actual late-2024 dollars, the payment was $2,149.
The dashed line asks a narrower question: what would the payment be at each quarter’s price if the rate stayed at 2.88%? It ends at $1,160. The gap between the lines shows how much the interest rate changes the payment at the same price; it does not predict where house prices would have gone if rates had stayed low.
Falling prices did help. They just did not bring this new borrower’s monthly payment close to its early-2021 level.
These figures cover new homes, whose median price can change when the mix of homes sold changes. They also leave out taxes, insurance, maintenance, fees, and income. This is a comparison of loan payments, not a complete measure of affordability. And an owner who already has a fixed-rate mortgage does not automatically face the higher rates shown here.
The distinction matters: a cheaper house can still come with a larger monthly bill.

title: Home prices fell, but mortgage payments stayed high
text:
Data and code
Freddie Mac changed its mortgage-rate survey methodology on November 17, 2022, which complicates comparisons across that date. The published averages are not the rate every individual buyer would receive.
I averaged 208 weekly mortgage rates and 48 monthly CPI observations within their calendar quarters, then joined them to 16 quarterly sale prices. The code checks completeness, missing values, and duplicate dates. For a loan with 360 monthly payments,
\[
M = 0.8P\frac{i}{1-(1+i)^{-360}}, \qquad i=\frac{r}{100\times12},
\]
where \(P\) is the sale price and \(r\) is the annual rate in percent. Multiplying prices and payments by \(\mathrm{CPI}_{2021\mathrm{Q1}}/\mathrm{CPI}_t\) expresses them in 2021 Q1 dollars. Calculations use unrounded rates.
Quarterly calculations (CSV) · Replication instructions · Analysis code
Sources, retrieved October 6, 2026:

U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States (MSPUS), via FRED. Dollars, quarterly, not seasonally adjusted.
Freddie Mac. 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (MORTGAGE30US), via FRED. Percent, weekly, not seasonally adjusted.
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average (CPIAUCSL), via FRED. Monthly, seasonally adjusted, 1982–1984 = 100.

The saved data were downloaded programmatically from FRED CSV URLs. Both the offline analysis and the --refresh download-and-analysis workflow were verified. Providers can revise historical data; the README documents the retrieval method and replication limits.

title: Where rent takes the biggest bite in Los Angeles
text:
In Los Angeles County tracts with median monthly gross rents of $2,500 or more, 54.0% of renter households spent at least 30% of their income on rent. In tracts with median rents between $1,500 and $1,999, the share was 60.0%.
Are the places with the highest rents also the places where tenants struggle most to pay them? I compared monthly rent with rent as a share of income. The distinction matters for housing assistance: monthly rents alone leave out how much tenants earn.
I used the Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 American Community Survey estimates for Los Angeles County. Census tracts are small statistical areas, rather than official neighborhood boundaries. These are rents paid by existing occupants, including covered utilities, not today’s advertised apartment prices. The comparisons exclude households for which the Census cannot calculate a rent-to-income ratio.

title: Where rent takes the biggest bite in Los Angeles
section: The expensive areas are easier to spot
text:
The expensive areas are easier to spot



Figure 1. Median monthly gross rent by census tract, in 2024 dollars. The main panel enlarges the urban area; the inset shows the full county and the enlarged area. Gray tracts have unavailable values or fewer than 100 estimated renter households with a computable rent-to-income ratio.


The county’s median monthly gross rent was $1,954. The map shows higher rents toward the coast and western parts of the urban area, with expensive tracts in some foothill communities too. Many central and southern tracts fall into lower rent categories.
This map shows what tenants pay each month. To see how much of their income goes toward that bill, we need a second measure.

title: Where rent takes the biggest bite in Los Angeles
section: The burden has a different geography
text:
The burden has a different geography



Figure 2. Share of renter households spending at least 30% of income on gross rent, among households with a computable ratio. The geographic extent and inclusion rule match Figure 1.


Countywide, 57.7% of eligible renter households spent at least 30% of income on gross rent, and 30.9% spent at least half.
Heavy burdens appear in many central and southern areas where rents are relatively modest, and in parts of the San Fernando Valley and northern county. Some expensive tracts have high burdens too. The pressure extends well beyond the high-rent areas along the coast.
Income helps explain why the two measures can differ. A hypothetical household earning $3,000 a month and paying $1,500 in gross rent spends half its income on housing. Another earning $10,000 and paying $2,500 spends a quarter. The more expensive home need not take the larger share of the household budget.

title: Where rent takes the biggest bite in Los Angeles
section: Even the cheaper areas face substantial pressure
text:
Even the cheaper areas face substantial pressure



Figure 3. Rent burdens pooled across households in four groups of tracts, classified by tract median gross rent. The 50% group is a subset of the 30% group. Whiskers show approximate 90% margins of error; they do not account for uncertainty in rent-band assignment.


I grouped tracts into four rent bands, then calculated the burdened share of households in each group. Each household counts equally, so a tract with more renters gets more weight than one with fewer.
The share spending at least 30% of income on rent exceeded half in every band. It was 59.1% in tracts with median rents below $1,500, compared with 54.0% in the $2,500-or-more group. The shares spending at least half their income were 32.3% and 28.0%, respectively.
These estimates describe areas and their current renters. They do not show what would happen to the same household if it moved, or establish that a particular tract is more affordable for a new arrival. Sampling error also makes close comparisons uncertain.
Housing assistance needs to reach renters in relatively low-rent areas too. Even in tracts with median rents below $1,500, nearly one in three eligible renter households spent at least half their income on rent. A map of monthly prices alone would miss much of that strain.

title: Where rent takes the biggest bite in Los Angeles
text:
Data and code
GitHub project and replication instructions · Tract calculations (CSV) · Rent-band results (CSV)
The analysis uses ACS tables B25064 and B25070, downloaded programmatically from the official 2024 table-based Summary Files, and 2024 Census cartographic tract boundaries. Retrieval date: October 19, 2026, Pacific time. Dollars in these five-year estimates are already adjusted to 2024 purchasing power.
For B25070, the denominator is total renter households minus the “not computed” category; that category includes no-rent-paid households and those with zero or negative income. The numerator sums the published bins beginning at 30%; the severe-burden numerator is the 50%-or-more bin. See the Census subject definitions.
Both maps and the grouped comparison retain 2,325 tracts with positive reported median rent and at least 100 estimated eligible renter households, covering 99.2% of the county’s eligible households. The cutoff is a stability rule, not a count of survey respondents. Lowering it to 50 changes each band’s burden rate by less than 0.1 percentage point. County benchmarks use the published county totals.
Boundaries join one-to-one on tract GEOID and use California Albers (EPSG:3310). Three ACS tracts omitted from the cartographic boundary file have zero renter households. Medians reported as $3,500+ remain open-ended; the map’s highest class starts at $3,000. Large polygons represent land area, not numbers of renters. Approximate margins of error follow Census guidance; grouped intervals ignore unavailable covariances and uncertainty in assigning tracts to rent bands.

title: Does one year’s pay tell the whole story?
text:
Does a single year’s pay tell us how closely children’s earnings track their mothers’? Using 822 children linked to 669 mothers, I find little change when I replace annual earnings with averages. Measuring children at different ages also changes the estimates, but those differences are uncertain.
This tutorial uses the NLSY79 and its Child/Young Adult study. Here, income means wages, salaries and military pay, rather than total household resources. Using the same definition avoids comparing a mother’s family budget with a child’s own paycheck. The notebook runs the complete Python and SQL workflow; the steps below explain the matching and comparisons.

title: Does one year’s pay tell the whole story?
text:
Build one row per child
Start with the identifiers. A child’s CPUBID identifies that child; MPUBID identifies their biological mother and matches her CASEID in NLSY79. Siblings share a mother ID. A household number alone cannot establish this relationship because household membership changes.
Python loads the extracts into SQLite, cleans missing codes and assigns amounts to the year earned. SQL adjusts earnings to 2020 dollars. From stage_income, summarize each person’s age window:
SELECT generation, person_id, stage,
       AVG(real_income) AS mean_income,
       COUNT(DISTINCT income_year) AS observed_years
FROM stage_income
GROUP BY generation, person_id, stage;
SELECT chooses columns; GROUP BY collects person-window records; AVG and COUNT calculate mean earnings and observed years. Save these as stage_averages. Then JOIN links each child to both generations’ summaries:
SELECT c.child_id, c.mother_id,
       m.mean_income AS mother_mean, a.mean_income AS adult_mean
FROM children AS c
JOIN stage_averages AS m
  ON m.person_id = c.mother_id AND m.stage = 'mother30s'
JOIN stage_averages AS a
  ON a.person_id = c.child_id AND a.stage = 'child30s';
Summarizing first prevents repeated survey years from multiplying matches. The full query applies eligibility rules and creates matched, with one row per child. Check that child IDs are unique after matching; duplicates would give some children extra weight in the regression.

title: Does one year’s pay tell the whole story?
text:
Compare annual earnings with averages
Compare the annual observation nearest age 35 with average earnings at ages 30–39. Mothers need at least three observed years; children need at least two. Years need not be consecutive. Average inflation-adjusted amounts before taking logs. Include genuine zeros in averages, exclude missing answers, and require positive measures for logarithms.
With pandas, NumPy and statsmodels imported, estimate the averaged model:
sample = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT * FROM matched", connection)
x = pd.DataFrame({
    "log_mother": np.log(sample.mother_mean),
    "mother_age": sample.mother_mean_age - 35,
    "child_age": sample.adult_mean_age - 35,
    "female": (sample.child_sex == 2).astype(int),
    "birth_year": sample.child_birth_year - 1978,
})
fit = sm.OLS(np.log(sample.adult_mean), sm.add_constant(x)).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": sample.mother_id},
    use_t=True)
The log_mother coefficient is the intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE). An estimate of 0.103 associates 10% higher maternal earnings with roughly 1.0% higher child earnings. This is an association, not a causal effect. Keep children and adjustments fixed across models; cluster uncertainty by mother because siblings share a parent.



Figure 1. IGE using annual or averaged earnings for the same 822 children. Bars show 95% confidence intervals clustered by mother.


Figure 1 gives 0.097 with annual earnings, 0.113 after averaging mothers’ earnings, and 0.103 after averaging both generations. The confidence interval for the change includes zero, so the difference is uncertain. Averaging spreads a temporary bonus or job loss across several observations, improving the proxy for longer-run earnings. It does not guarantee a higher IGE.

title: Does one year’s pay tell the whole story?
text:
Check the child’s age
Hold maternal averages and adjustments fixed. Select each child’s annual observation nearest the midpoint of each five-year band, from 20–24 to 35–39. Keep the same children throughout, so changing participants cannot explain differences.



Figure 2. IGE at four child-age bands, holding maternal averages fixed. The sample and confidence-interval method match Figure 1.


The estimates are 0.063, 0.125, 0.097, 0.129, in age order. The oldest-minus-youngest confidence interval includes zero, so the apparent age difference is uncertain. Haider and Solon explain the life-cycle problem: people with higher lifetime earnings can have faster earnings growth, so early earnings can understate eventual differences. Figure 2 checks sensitivity to age; it cannot measure bias against unobserved lifetime income.
Check both how many income observations were used and when they were measured. Averaging addresses short-term fluctuations; it does not automatically fix life-cycle bias.
These unweighted results describe selected families with repeated observations and positive selected annual earnings in every age band. They are not national mobility estimates. Earnings exclude self-employment, and age changes alongside calendar time.

title: How much extra did 15 gallons cost in California?
text:
A difference of a dollar per gallon can look small on a gas-station sign. For a 15-gallon purchase, it adds $15 to the bill. I wanted to put California’s price difference in these everyday terms: from 2020 through 2025, how much more did the same 15 gallons cost in California than at the U.S. average price?
Across 313 weekly observations, the extra cost averaged $17.59. California’s price was higher in every observed week. But that average hides a wide range: the extra cost ran from $11.84 to $36.47, depending on the date.

title: How much extra did 15 gallons cost in California?
text:
Making the comparison fair
I use the Energy Information Administration’s weekly California and U.S. prices for regular gasoline, all formulations, including taxes. Matching the same date and grade avoids comparing different products or different weeks. There are no missing dates in the matched series.
Fifteen gallons is a fixed comparison quantity, not an estimate of anyone’s tank size or fuel use. For each week, I calculate:
Extra for 15 gallons = 15 × (California price − U.S. price).
The national average includes California. It therefore provides a familiar benchmark, rather than the average for the other 49 states. The overall result gives each observed week equal weight; it does not estimate the average driver’s spending.
Start with the full period below, then choose a year. The average and the lowest and highest weeks update together. Hover over the line, or use the observation selector, to inspect the prices behind any point.


Figure 1. Extra cost at California’s average price relative to the U.S. average, January 6, 2020–December 29, 2025. Both views use the same 313 weekly observations.

title: How much extra did 15 gallons cost in California?
section: Was the extra cost similar every year?
text:
Was the extra cost similar every year?
Choosing 2020 gives an average extra cost of $13.23. Choosing 2025 raises it to $19.68. For the same quantity of gasoline, the average difference was $6.45 larger in 2025. The annual average was highest in 2022, at $20.39.
All amounts are nominal dollars: they describe the dollar gap at the time, without adjusting for inflation. They do not show whether the extra cost took a larger share of someone’s income. That would require income and fuel-use data.

title: How much extra did 15 gallons cost in California?
section: The highest pump price was not the largest gap
text:
The highest pump price was not the largest gap
The most revealing comparison is within 2022. On June 13, 2022, California’s price reached its highest level in this dataset, $6.271 per gallon. The U.S. average was $5.006, so the extra cost for 15 gallons was $18.98.
By October 3, 2022, California’s price had edged down to $6.213. Meanwhile, the U.S. average had fallen to $3.782. The extra cost reached $36.47, the largest weekly gap in the six-year period. California gasoline was slightly cheaper than in June, yet its premium over the national price was much larger.
Select 2022 and switch the chart view to pump prices to see why. The two lines show the comparison that the extra-cost line summarizes. Zooming into June through October makes this change easier to inspect. The interaction lets me check how a period average changes when I include or exclude the spike.

title: How much extra did 15 gallons cost in California?
section: What I take from the chart
text:
What I take from the chart
The evidence answers how large the difference was and when it widened. It does not identify its causes. EIA discusses taxes, fuel specifications, transport and supply conditions as contributors to regional prices, but these two series cannot separate their effects.
EIA’s survey notes describe Monday morning cash prices, generally self-service, with volume weights within each area. These are estimates, not prices at every station. The minimum and maximum show variation over dates, not a confidence interval.
My takeaway is straightforward: over 2020–2025, buying the same 15 gallons at California’s average price cost about $17.59 more than at the U.S. average. To understand that difference, I need both prices. A falling California price alone does not tell me whether the extra cost is shrinking.
Download the weekly calculations, code and data, or see the replication instructions.

title: Does working from home mean staying home all week?
text:
Someone who works from home for a few hours on Friday and someone who stays home all week can both be counted as teleworkers. That makes “working from home” a surprisingly broad label. Before drawing conclusions about how much work has moved home, it helps to ask how much of the working week people actually spend there.
Among U.S. workers who worked from home in 2024, was it more common to do all their work at home or only some of it?
I used all twelve 2024 Basic Monthly samples from IPUMS CPS, covering civilians ages 16 and older who worked during the survey reference week. The survey asks whether they worked from home for pay, how many hours they did so, and their total hours worked. I applied the person-level WTFINL weights so that the results describe the population rather than just the respondents.

title: Does working from home mean staying home all week?
section: A little over half combined home and other working hours
text:
A little over half combined home and other working hours






Figure 1: Shares of people at work, ages 16 and older. All figures use IPUMS CPS weights.



Across 2024, about 22.8% of people at work did at least some paid work from home. Figure 1 separates that group into people who worked only some hours at home and those who worked every hour there. Both groups were much smaller than the group doing no telework.
Among teleworkers whose hours could be classified, 52.3% worked only some hours at home, while 47.7% worked all their hours there. The split was close. A slight majority had a mixed week, but working entirely from home was also common. Calling every teleworker fully remote would overlook more than half of this group.

title: Does working from home mean staying home all week?
section: A remote week could contain very different amounts of home working
text:
A remote week could contain very different amounts of home working






Figure 2: Distribution of the share of actual working hours spent at home, among teleworkers with valid hours.



For each teleworker, I divided hours worked at home by total hours worked that week. Someone who worked 40 hours in total and 16 hours at home, for example, would have a home-working share of 40%.
Figure 2 shows why the yes-or-no telework question leaves considerable variation hidden. About 31.3% of teleworkers spent less than half their working time at home. Others spent most of their week there, and the largest single category worked entirely from home. Sharing the same teleworker label therefore tells us relatively little about two people’s weekly routines.
These are shares of hours, so they cannot tell us how many whole days someone stayed home. A few hours at home each evening could add up to the same total as two complete days.

title: Does working from home mean staying home all week?
section: The close split appeared throughout the year
text:
The close split appeared throughout the year






Figure 3: Monthly share of teleworkers doing only some hours at home. The dashed line marks an equal split.



The annual result could conceal differences across months. Figure 3 checks this by calculating the split separately for each survey month. The partial-home group had the larger point estimate in all twelve months. July was almost evenly divided at 50.2%; December’s estimate was 53.9%.
These monthly estimates are not seasonally adjusted, and I have not tested whether the small differences are statistically significant. The useful finding is how close the two groups remained, rather than a claim that preferences changed during the year.
The main takeaway is that paid work at home often occupied only part of a person’s working week. Debates about workplace attendance should make that distinction explicit. The CPS records what happened during one reference week; it does not identify a permanent hybrid contract, the location of the remaining hours, or whether someone preferred that arrangement.
